p0003_00.text: John Keells Holdings PLC For over 150 years, John Keells Group has been at the leading edge of Sri Lankan business and industry; cutting through convention, exploring new horizons and exceeding expectations to connect people with products and services that exemplify excellence in every detail. The most capital-intensive phase of our recent investment cycle now draws to a close and we accelerate into the next phase with increasing momentum, all the while maintaining our focus on prudent capital stewardship, operational excellence and long-term perspective. In the past, we have discussed our portfolio strategies involving several major investments anticipated to produce long-term returns. We have also explained the measurable impacts we have observed across our businesses through our data analytics practices, which have resulted in transformative impact and customer value. This year, we let our numbers speak for themselves, as the Group achieved an EBITDA of Rs.80.01 billion, an increase of 75%. This notable achievement was driven by improved operating outcomes, broad-based earnings and strong returns, combined with consistent value creation from our established businesses. Our portfolio is positioned to optimally deliver long-term value and we look forward to an exciting journey ahead, notwithstanding the headwinds we face as a country and across the world. p0011_00.text: CHAIRPERSON'S MESSAGE The year under review reflected meaningful progress for the Group, underpinned by strong financial performance and encouraging momentum across new initiatives and ventures. p0043_00.text: OPERATING ENVIRONMENT This section covers the Group's external operating landscape from an economic, political and regulatory, environmental and social, and technological standpoint, and the resultant impacts on the Group during the year. Key Takeaways (i) Global growth remained resilient in CY2025, supported by technology-led investment, while inflation moderated. (ii) Sri Lanka sustained a real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth of 5.0% for the second consecutive year, underpinned by macro stabilisation and policy reforms, with fiscal upside due to the relaxation of vehicle import restrictions. (iii) Accommodative domestic monetary conditions and improving confidence supported a broad-based recovery in demand, benefiting consumer-facing and interest-sensitive businesses. (iv) External buffers strengthened (including higher reserves) but renewed geopolitical tensions in late February 2026 increased downside risks in Sri Lanka in relation to energy, freight, tourism and remittances, in particular, pointing to a more volatile and higher-cost operating environment into CY2026. (v) Climate-related disruptions and sustainability reporting requirements continued to elevate resilience, preparedness and data maturity as strategic priorities. GLOBAL ENVIRONMENT Global economic growth saw a modest uptick to 3.4% in CY2025, compared to 3.3% in CY2024, demonstrating resilience despite tariff barriers and elevated policy uncertainty. This momentum was sustained by strong technology-related investment, including in artificial intelligence (AI) and supported by the commencement of accommodative monetary policy conditions. Given the stable demand conditions and reasonable supply conditions, global inflation moderated to 4.1% in CY2025 compared to 4.2% in CY2024. Among advanced economies, growth continued to be led by the United States (US), albeit at a slower pace than in CY2024, as technology investment remained supportive while higher trade barriers, policy uncertainty and

p0043_01.text: growth continued to be led by the United States (US), albeit at a slower pace than in CY2024, as technology investment remained supportive while higher trade barriers, policy uncertainty and moderating labour market momentum weighed on growth compared to the previous year. The World Economic Forum's Global Risks Report identifies extreme weather–related risks, both acute events (such as floods, storms and heatwaves) and chronic climate-related changes (including rising temperatures, sea level rise and prolonged drought) as the single most severe global risk over the long term, highlighting the growing systemic impacts of climate change on economies and societies. During the reporting period, Sri Lanka experienced a significant climate-related event when Cyclone Ditwah impacted the country in late November 2025, resulting in an estimated USD 4.1 billion in physical damage, primarily to transportation infrastructure, as reported by the World Bank. The event significantly disrupted livelihoods, essential services and broader economic activity, reinforcing the critical importance of strengthening disaster preparedness and climate resilience. Responsible resource management and climate resilience remained areas of focus during the year, with initiatives across industry groups addressing emissions, energy, water, waste and biodiversity, alongside continued emphasis on extended product responsibility through programmes such as Plasticcycle, Gunadamin and Good Water. Refer Natural Capital Review for further details on sustainability initiatives – page 65. The Group experienced short term operational disruptions during and in the immediate aftermath of the cyclone, including temporary outlet closures in affected areas within the Supermarket business and cold chain-related disruptions in the Confectionery business. Despite this, there were no material operational or financial impacts arising directly from the cyclone and associated flooding. p0139_00.text: OUTLOOK AND RISKS This section outlines the evolving operating environment, the Group's approach to navigating it, and the implications for the Group's outlook and way forward. The discussion comprises three parts: • Macroeconomic Outlook from both global and local perspectives. • Group Outlook which sets out the Group's key strategic focus areas and the macroeconomic implications on the Group. • Key Risks to the Group's outlook based on those identified through the Group's Enterprise Risk Management framework. MACROECONOMIC OUTLOOK Global Context The global economy was envisaged to sustain the growth momentum observed in CY2025, supported by continued investments in artificial intelligence (AI) and related technologies, which are likely to partly offset the impact of trade barriers and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty. However, the escalation of tensions in the Middle East since late February 2026 has introduced renewed uncertainty, tempering the outlook for CY2026. The escalation of conflict in the Middle East since 28 February 2026, has emerged as a significant geopolitical development, with implications across the region and beyond. The developments heightened risks across energy-producing economies, with impacts on infrastructure, production capacity, trade and investor sentiment. A key source of impact has been the disruption to the Strait of Hormuz, a strategically critical conduit for global energy flows, where restricted access has led to a contraction in shipping activity, affecting supply chains and contributing to increased volatility in energy markets. In addition, spillover effects across the region have resulted in disruptions to air connectivity across key Middle Eastern transit hubs. These developments have also contributed to increased volatility across global financial markets, resulting in risk aversion, capital flow adjustments, and currency pressures, particularly in emerging markets. While a ceasefire reached in early April 2026 provided some

p0139_01.text: global financial markets, resulting in risk aversion, capital flow adjustments, and currency pressures, particularly in emerging markets. While a ceasefire reached in early April 2026 provided some prospects of de-escalation, subsequent developments point to continued underlying tensions and volatility. Constraints on maritime transit and intermittent disruptions highlight the evolving nature of the current situation, with a sustained resolution yet to be achieved. While the outlook remains uncertain, the gradual restoration of critical trade flows and easing of disruptions will be key in supporting stability in global markets. Conflict in the Middle East In light of the prevailing Middle East conflict, the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) April 2026 World Economic Outlook reflects a moderation in global growth, with global GDP growth projected at 3.1% in CY2026, revised down from the 3.3% forecast in January 2026 under the assumption that the conflict remains relatively contained in duration and scale. Growth is expected to recover modestly to 3.2% in CY2027 supported by continued investment in technology and productivity improvements, although this will depend on what transpires in CY2026 and the status of the conflict. The impact of this moderation is expected to be more pronounced in the conflict-affected region, as well as in commodity-importing emerging markets and developing economies with pre-existing structural and macroeconomic vulnerabilities. Policy responses across major economies are expected to remain data-dependent, as central banks balance inflation risks with the need to support growth, potentially resulting in divergent monetary policy paths. p0140_00.text: The Middle East conflict is expected to affect the Sri Lankan economy through several key channels, particularly through higher energy and fuel prices. While elevated fuel costs will contribute to inflationary pressures and a widening trade deficit, domestic pricing adjustments and demand management measures are expected to help mitigate these impacts, to an extent. Foreign remittances, a key source of foreign exchange inflows, particularly from the Middle East, may moderate in a prolonged conflict scenario, while softer tourism earnings could contribute to some variability in the exchange rate, especially in the event of renewed disruptions to regional air connectivity. Broader global uncertainty may also soften external demand, while disruptions to trade flows and elevated logistics costs could affect export performance, with some transmission to sectors such as agriculture through higher input costs. The elevated global fuel oil prices will place a significant strain on the total import bill of the country and also result in a cascading impact on prices. While export and service flows have been resilient, the increase in the import bill and resultant trade deficit will place pressure on the currency, as seen recently. The flexible exchange rate policy adopted by the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) has resulted the depreciation of the currency, as seen in many economies in the region, which will also compound the impact on prices. Collectively, these developments are likely to influence Sri Lanka's economic trajectory across growth, inflation, external balances, and exchange rate dynamics. The overall impact will depend on the extent and duration of disruptions to energy and trade flows, as well as the timeliness and effectiveness of policy responses to evolving external conditions. p0156_00.text: STRATEGY, RESOURCE ALLOCATION AND PORTFOLIO MANAGEMENT HURDLE RATE OF JKH The present hurdle rate of JKH is 15%, which is a function of the weighted average cost of capital (WACC). The WACC is derived from the Group's cost of equity, cost of debt, target capital structure, tax rates and the value creation premium required over and above the WACC. Given the stable macroeconomic indicators, the Group maintained its hurdle rate at the same level during the current year. This rate serves as the initial benchmark in evaluating project feasibility, with projectspecific modifiers applied to provide a more granular assessment. For example, a risk modifier is applied to investments with high foreign currency exposure, using a project-specific cost of debt and equity return benchmark. This is then compared against projects with similar risk profiles. The Group will continue to assess evolving economic conditions and geopolitical uncertainties to determine whether revisions to the long term hurdle rate are necessary. This transition is important because it will gradually improve the correlation between earnings and the enhanced capital base over the medium term. In the short to medium term, the Group's priority will be to extract full value from these investments by accelerating ramp-up, improving utilisation, and enhancing yields across CODSL and WCT-1. p0159_02.text: Sri Lankan Equity Market Review The Sri Lankan equity market recorded a strong performance during CY2025, supported by improving macroeconomic stability, easing financial conditions, and a sustained recovery in corporate earnings. The All Share Price Index (ASPI) and the S&P Sri Lanka 20 Index broadly reflected this positive backdrop, closing the year at 22,624 points and 6,157 points, respectively, representing gains of ~42% and 27%.
